articles.description: Elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have dealt the CDU a historic defeat while the AfD saw a massive gain. The pressure on Germany's unpopular chancellor is mounting.
articles.title: German state elections deal a blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz

articles.description: Despite making significant gains in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right AfD remains without options to form a state government.
articles.title: AfD makes gains in state elections but has no government options

articles.description: The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue for the government. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation infrastructure.
articles.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise

articles.description: A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.
articles.title: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners

articles.description: Oktoberfest 2026 is underway but it's not just beer on offer in Munich this year; revelers can also get themselves a flu jab before heading to the tents. DW has more.
articles.title: Germany news: Doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs

articles.description: The summer of 2026 was not only the hottest on record in Europe, it also saw a record number of people die. More than 16,000 are thought to have died because of the heat in Germany alone.
articles.title: Summer of 2026 broke records in Europe, and caused deaths

articles.description: This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!
articles.title: Oktoberfest 2026: Everything you need to know

articles.description: Bloody May, student sit-ins and the squatter movement: Berlin has long been a hotbed for working-class organizing and radical left-wing politics.
articles.title: Rebels, workers, radicals: The making of 'Red Berlin'

articles.description: Women's football is growing rapidly, particularly in Germany. Nevertheless, equal pay and investment remain major talking points.
articles.title: Women's football in Germany booming, but still much to do

articles.description: As war disrupts one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, satellite images reveal that oil is spreading toward protected coral reefs and mangrove forests.
articles.title: Strait of Hormuz attacks spill oil into Persian Gulf

articles.description: Coach Jürgen Klopp has named several players to his first Germany squad who are eligible to play for other countries. Some still aren't committed to playing for thje national team long-term.
articles.title: Dual citizenship means Germany now in competition for talent

articles.description: The new exhibition "Beethoven by Warhol" at the Beethoven House in Bonn presents the pop artist's late masterpiece: a picture of Ludwig van Beethoven. The exhibition shares the story of the work with the public.
articles.title: Beethoven and Andy Warhol: Rebel icons on show in Bonn

articles.description: After a decade of use, questions around VAR in football are louder than ever. Has the technology strayed too far from its remit?
articles.title: VAR's mission creep a problem for football

articles.description: Ice hockey legend Alexander Ovechkin has lent Vladimir Putin's party a helping hand in its parliamentary election campaign. That's in keeping with a pattern of support by an athlete who claims not to be political.
articles.title: Alexander Ovechkin backs Putin party in campaign video

articles.description: Jürgen Klopp, Germany's new head coach, says he wants his team to reclaim pride in being German after recent political developments.
articles.title: Klopp wants Germany's football team to 'reclaim the flag'

articles.description: Time and again, residents tracing the history of their homes discover the lives of Jewish predecessors who fled or were deported amid stories of suffering and loss.
articles.title: Jews once lived lived here: When houses tell stories

articles.description: Germany's new head coach Jürgen Klopp has named a huge squad for his first four games, splitting them into two groups. A host of new faces is included.
articles.title: Jürgen Klopp's first Germany squad includes 44 players

articles.description: From "Apostle of the Apostles" to prostitute, Mary Magdalene has been assigned a wide variety of roles, as a new exhibition shows.
articles.title: Saint, sinner or feminist icon: How Mary Magdalene's image evolved through time

articles.description: A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.
articles.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse

articles.description: Following Manuel Neuer's retirement, there are many candidates to succeed him, but which goalkeeper will Jürgen Klopp choose? What factors will play a role? And will Neuer's future have an indirect influence?
articles.title: After Neuer: Who will be Germany's new No. 1 goalkeeper?

articles.description: Two decades of progress toward gender parity is at risk as women's political representation declines, according to a new World Economic Forum report. At the current pace, the remaining gap could take 120 years to close.
articles.title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'

articles.description: A decade after the terrorist attack on a Berlin Christmas market, a new German miniseries looks into the institutional failures that allowed the deadly truck rampage to happen.
articles.title: German drama 'Blindspot Berlin' revisits 2016 Christmas market attack

articles.description: Heat waves, wildfires and floods have cascading economic impacts, causing incomes to decline and the price of basic goods to rise. The trend will escalate as temperatures continue to increase.
articles.title: How extreme heat is hitting wallets

articles.description: Paleontologists in Spain say they have found the first evidence of the long-necked Diplodocus genus of dinosaur outside of North America. They found bones at the rich La Tejeria fossil site in Teruel in eastern Spain.
articles.title: Spanish scientists find first evidence of Diplodocus dinosaur in Europe

articles.description: US debt has topped $40 trillion. How risky is the country's growing debt burden. And will investors keep funding Washington's deficits?
articles.title: Why the era of cheap government debt is over

articles.description: Could artificial intelligence pose an existential threat to humanity? Some leading researchers are warning against an unregulated race toward AI superintelligence.
articles.title: Why AI researchers warn humanity could face extinction

articles.description: The pistachios sold across the United States have a surprising history: California's trees trace their roots to Iran. Now, both regions face the same threat — their farmland is sinking as groundwater disappears.
articles.title: Iran and US: Two countries and the pistachio between them

articles.description: Germany thrilled fans at the Women's Basketball World Cup. But even if this sparked a boom in the women's game, the infrastructure simply isn't ready for it.
articles.title: Women's Basketball World Cup: Can Germany harness a boom?

articles.description: Dangote seeks $1.6 billion from investors to finance a $14.3 billion expansion and thus double the oil refinery's capacity. The offer could give millions of Nigerians a stake in the company. But who can truly afford it?
articles.title: Africa's richest man Dangote's IPO out of reach in Nigeria

articles.description: In 1095, the Catholic Church launched the Crusades: wars that left millions dead and whose legacy still shapes political and ideological conflicts.
articles.title: The Crusades: How a medieval holy war still shapes politics

articles.description: Iran is shifting trade toward northern ports and land routes as its southern shipping faces a US blockade. Analysts say the corridors can keep essential goods moving, but cannot replace maritime trade.
articles.title: Can Iran replace sea trade with land routes?

articles.description: Alexander Zverev has won the US Open for the first time, defeating Ben Shelton in the final. It is Zverev's second Grand Slam win of 2026 after a long wait for his first title, but controversy still hangs over him.
articles.title: Germany's Zverev wins US Open in golden year

articles.description: The Netherlands and France have moved their gold out of US vaults. Part of the reason is fears about the reliability of the US, but equally important is the need to keep gold closer to home in the event of a crisis.
articles.title: Why are European banks moving gold out of United States?

articles.description: Records show that El Nino events have been frequent and often extreme over the past few decades. Is this normal? Or is it the result of climate change? Corals can give us a clear indication.
articles.title: Corals as climate archive: Are El Nino events intensifying?

articles.description: The BRICS summit 2026 takes place in Delhi this weekend. Unlike last year, Putin and Xi are expected to attend. Can India keep the expanded bloc united?
articles.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn

articles.description: The Goethe-Institut was one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia. However, following Moscow's decision to close its offices, all employees will have to stop working by September 13.
articles.title: The 'end of an era' as Goethe-Institut in Russia closes

articles.description: As the global star kicks off her anticipated Paris residency, here's how Celine Dion managed to gain younger followers while keeping her loyal older fans.
articles.title: How Celine Dion became a pop culture icon across generations

articles.description: The documentary "Letters from the Silenced Country" depicts the ongoing repression under the authoritarian regime. Director Andrei Kutsila talked to DW ahead of the film's Venice premiere.
articles.title: How Belarusians still find hope in a silenced country

articles.description: When physicists said they may have spotted evidence of dark matter almost 100 years after it was proposed as a theory, the internet lit up. Here's why we're searching for the thing that holds everything else together.
articles.title: Why we're still looking for dark matter

articles.description: Six months after Saudi Arabia pulled funding from the breakaway organization, LIV Golf have filed for bankruptcy protection. Several of the world's best players signed on to LIV, so where does that leave golf?
articles.title: LIV Golf in financial turmoil: What's next for the sport?

articles.description: Twenty-five years after 9/11, conspiracy theories about the terrorist attacks persist. But even as an attempt to make sense of a tragedy, psychologists say the benefit in conspiracy ideation or belief is short-lived.
articles.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers but not peace

articles.description: Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, using suitcases on planes and legal loopholes to deliver them to dinnerplates. Where are the smuggling hotspots?
articles.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction

articles.description: The exhibition of the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum is eagerly anticipated across the UK, as the medieval masterpiece is considered by many to be a symbol of the country's identity.
articles.title: The Bayeux Tapestry in London: What's behind the hype?

articles.description: The PISA 2025 results reveal record-low student performance, with digital distractions and AI use raising concerns. Germany is faring worse than ever.
articles.title: PISA 2025 results: Reading and math scores plummet worldwide

articles.description: As his latest movie, "Bucking Fastard," premiered at the Venice Film Festival, DW talked to the boundary-breaking director.
articles.title: Werner Herzog: Germany's wild man of cinema is back

articles.description: The Zagreb demonstrators demanded that the government come up with a plan to clear illegal toxic waste in 20 days. Prime Minister Plenkovic has promised to tackle the issue.
articles.title: Croatia: Toxic waste protest draws tens of thousands

articles.description: Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. But over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.
articles.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination

articles.description: As data centers multiply to meet AI demand, they're straining power grids, draining water supplies and reshaping the land and air around them.
articles.title: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers

articles.description: Germany's far-right AfD party has long claimed that the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt has been left behind. Is that really the case? A closer look at the data offers some interesting insights.
articles.title: Germany: Is Saxony-Anhalt's economy really struggling?

articles.description: The motto of this year's classical music festival in Bonn is "Home/At Home," featuring musicians from diverse cultures presenting pieces from their homelands.
articles.title: 2026 Beethoven Festival evokes a sense of home

articles.description: The struggling German carmaker plans to cut up to 100,000 jobs from its 630,000-strong workforce. How did VW's headcount get so bloated, and will the cuts be enough to survive the Chinese EV onslaught?
articles.title: How Volkswagen's huge workforce became a costly burden

articles.description: Despite a slew of negative headlines, the German economy has posted its best figures in years. There are reasons for optimism, but structural issues remain.
articles.title: Is Germany's economic slump finally over?

articles.author: Nick Visser
articles.description:
Follow the day’s news live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Sydney man has been charged after allegedly restraining, choking and sexually assaulting a young woman in a park, Australian Associated Press reports.
A 23-year-old woman was walking from Flemington Station through Airey Park in Homebush, in Sydney’s west, around 11.15pm on Friday 18 September when she was stopped by a man not known to her, police say.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australia news live: Labor to make it harder for international students to change courses; Inman-Grant says time for new eSafety leadership

articles.author: Robert Mackey (now); Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
articles.description:
Justices will consider whether immigrants have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation

Sign up for the Breaking News US email

The White House has, again, blocked CNN from covering Donald Trump as part of the rotating press pool.
The outlet was scheduled to be a part of the group of media traveling to Texas and Oklahoma with the president today, but was removed from list of newsrooms in place for the trip, per the White House schedule.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump doesn’t rule out sending ICE to polling sites; US supreme court to review policy to detain immigrants challenging deportation – live

articles.author: Press Association
articles.description:
Rock band will still tour the UK, Europe and US over the next year but say decision to ‘fall dormant’ feels ‘liberating’
The British rock band Enter Shikari have announced they will go on hiatus at the end of 2027, a decision that may result in the band’s “extinction”.
The St Albans band, who formed in 1999 as Hybryd, are due to tour the UK in November, Europe and the US next year, and said they hoped to play some of their favourite places “one last time”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Enter Shikari announce indefinite hiatus from 2027: ‘We don’t think we’re splitting up’

articles.author: Patrick Greenfield
articles.description:
After five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be done
In the early autumn sunlight, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh’s extensive plant collection appears safe in their glass enclosures. But danger lurks from above for the tropical ferns, cycads and rare alpine heathers.
Soon the September sunshine will give way to the storms and gales of the Scottish winter, which can bring hundreds of glass panels crashing to the greenhouse floor on the windiest days. Nobody is allowed inside when the wind is above 30mph.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Falling glass and ‘decapitated’ plants: the race to protect Edinburgh botanic garden’s plants

articles.author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
articles.description:
Landlords can no longer refuse pit bulls, rottweilers, dobermans or other breeds considered ‘scary’
Landlords in Washington DC will no longer be able to refuse a tenant’s dog based on its breed, size or weight, nor can they impose special charges related to these factors.
At least, that’s what a new law that took effect on Thursday aims to achieve. Animal welfare organizations and animal shelters applauded the legislation, emphasizing the benefits of reducing barriers to pet ownership in the US capital.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New Washington DC law bans landlords from imposing dog breed restrictions

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Democratic-led coalition says gutting key protections will set US back decades and worsen climate crisis
States and cities sued the Trump administration on Thursday for repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas.
Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule. The Democratic-led coalition also includes Pennsylvania’s governor, the District of Columbia, New York City, Chicago and the city and county of Denver. They argue that “gutting one of the country’s most significant climate protections” will set the nation back decades and worsen the climate crisis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US states and cities sue over Trump EPA’s repeal of emissions rules

articles.author: Abené Clayton
articles.description:
MLB reportedly contacted White House about staging game at Wyoming park, to dismay of  locals and conservationists 
A proposal to hold a Major League Baseball (MLB) game inside a national park is receiving backlash from locals and conservationists.
On 26 September, the Washington Post reported that MLB reached out to the White House about staging a one-day game at the Grand Teton national park in Wyoming. Teton county describes itself as a “a year-round resort community” and sits within the Jackson Hole valley. It’s also a habitat for grizzly bears, osprey, bison and more.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Proposal to hold Major League Baseball game in Grand Teton national park sparks backlash

articles.author: Richard Luscombe
articles.description:
Independent inquiry ordered after failed execution of Pike, who was convicted of 1994 murder

Christa Pike: what we know so far about Tennessee woman’s failed execution

Tennessee’s governor on Thursday said it was “deeply disturbing” that his state botched the execution of a death row prisoner who remained alive and snoring 40 minutes after receiving a double dose of the lethal drug that should have quickly killed her.
Bill Lee, a Republican, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry after Wednesday night’s failed attempt to put to death Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder, at the execution chamber in Nashville.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tennessee suspends executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says failed lethal injection leaves her in critical condition

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Planned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’
Airlines will be blocked from charging parents extra to sit with their children on planes, according to government plans.
The new rule would require airlines to seat passengers aged under 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge. Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking if they need to correct a mistake.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with children

articles.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
articles.description:
PM has praised Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester, but critics say this ignores public cost of city’s transformation
In July 2016, the Manchester City player Yaya Touré ambled into a small bar near Beijing’s Workers’ Stadium and offered a bemused smile as dozens of Chinese fans rushed towards him.
Manchester City had just won their sixth trophy under the big-spending ownership of Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group and the blues were international megastars. They were also magnets for investment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How success of Manchester City helped put Andy Burnham in power

articles.author: Rowena Mason, Pippa Crerar and Patrick Butler
articles.description:
Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment
Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work, the Guardian has learned.
Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes

articles.author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro, Andrew Roth and Joseph Gedeon in Washington
articles.description:
Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls
Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after a Guardian report revealed how the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court.
Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed

articles.author: Jon Henley in Paris
articles.description:
About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country
A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting

articles.author: Peter Beaumont
articles.description:
Team behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systems
The team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s targeting policies in Gaza and its alleged acceptance of high numbers of civilian deaths, have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
The disclosure came in response to an Israel Defense Forces statement seeking to discredit the documentary.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in Gaza

articles.author: Alex Daniel
articles.description:
Ministers discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US supplies
Britain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.
Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Britain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpiles

articles.author: Jakub Krupa (now and earlier) and Martin Belam (earlier)
articles.description:
The president said it was a warning if any countries were considering an attack on Russia
The ⁠EU Commission, France, Italy, Ireland ⁠and ⁠Britain are ​holding a call on ⁠the possible need to release diesel ⁠stocks, an ​EU ‌official ‌said, as reported by Reuters.
A ‌Commission spokesperson had earlier declined direct comment on reports that the ‌Trump administration has told Germany and ​France to draw down emergency diesel ⁠inventories to help to ​ease global ​fuel ​prices or ​face ‌a potential ​US ​diesel export ban.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Putin says ‘all weapons at disposal’ if there’s an attack on Russia – as it happened

articles.author: William Christou and Jonathan Yerushalmy
articles.description:
Alleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opens
The Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has claimed.
Israeli passengers intervened to stop the attack on Wednesday, restraining the co-pilot, while a reserve crew in the plane was able to stabilise the plummeting plane and ultimately land it safely in Saudi Arabia.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Co-pilot in flight stabbing had ‘Islamic radical indoctrination’, says Netanyahu

articles.author: Joanna Partridge
articles.description:
Alternative ways being used to move fuel out of Gulf region, but flows of refined products such as diesel still constrained
Exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.
Pipeline exports and ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used, according to analysts tracking the situation, while the US military continues to escort some vessels. However, flows of refined products such as diesel remain constrained, pushing prices higher.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Crude oil exports from strait of Hormuz largely return to pre-war levels

articles.author: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science
articles.description:
Melbourne researchers behind previous BV transmission breakthrough turn attention to understanding why some cases are harder to cure 
Australian scientists have identified two contributors to recurrent bacterial vaginosis infections, a common sexual health condition that affects about one in four women globally.
The condition, commonly called BV, is characterised by an imbalance of naturally occurring bacteria in the vagina, in which there is a reduction of “good” bacteria and an overgrowth of other mixed bacteria.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Underlying causes of recurrent bacterial vaginosis identified by Australian scientists

articles.author: Henry Belot
articles.description:
One executive received a $1.5m package last year, while 10 other staff received remuneration exceeding $1m each

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Nearly a dozen federal public servants were paid more than $1m last year, with one receiving a $1.5m package worth more than double Anthony Albanese’s base salary.
The generous remuneration – which includes bonuses and allowances – has been criticised as insulting during a cost-of-living crisis and amid job cuts across the public service.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Million-dollar public servants: 11 staff at Australia’s Future Fund paid significantly more than the PM

articles.author: Adam Morton, Graham Readfearn and Penry Buckley
articles.description:
Exclusive: Climate Change Authority chair says planning commission did not account for climate-related economic damage in NSW

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

A senior Albanese government climate adviser has challenged the state approval of the largest coalmining development in New South Wales’s history, arguing “climate change isn’t someone else’s problem”.
Matt Kean, the chair of the Climate Change Authority and a former NSW treasurer and energy minister, questioned why the state Independent Planning Commission had not weighed the economic cost of climate change caused by burning the coal from the Hunter Valley Operations mine before giving it the green light to run until 2045.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Matt Kean warns climate crisis ‘isn’t someone else’s problem’ as largest coal project in NSW history greenlit

articles.author: Josh Butler
articles.description:
Maker of Claude claims AI could transform economy but ABC and SBS say the technology should be subject to media regulations

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The AI giant Anthropic has urged the Albanese government to consider giving “conditional approval” for big tech to train its models on Australian copyrighted works under an opt-out model, after conceding it won’t secure a blanket copyright exemption.
But Australia’s public broadcasters, the ABC and SBS, have strongly criticised AI firms, calling on the government to enact strict new rules to compensate media organisations and protect public interest journalism.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anthropic pushes for opt-out model for Australian content as ABC warns of ‘cannibalisation’ of news

articles.author: Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent
articles.description:
Police investigating reports of politicians’ homes being broken into in last year with nothing being stolen
The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, has said a foreign power could be responsible for a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of several members of parliament.
Police said on Thursday they were investigating multiple reports of MPs’ homes being broken into in the Helsinki area in the last year in which nothing was stolen but subtle signs of breaking and entering were left.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Finnish PM says suspected break-ins at MPs’ homes could be work of foreign power

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Indian government issued with warning it would be in contempt of court if it failed to release Jagtar Singh Johal
The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British Sikh activist released from Delhi jail after nine-year detention

articles.author: Pjotr Sauer in Kyiv
articles.description:
US president blames attacks for driving up fuel prices before midterms, though analysts say his Iran war is main cause

Europe live – latest updates

Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices.
Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. The Ukrainian president added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes in defiance of Trump

articles.author: Camille Rodríguez Montilla in Caracas and Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
articles.description:
Diehard Hugo Chávez supporters struggle to comprehend ideological U-turn being executed by Delcy Rodríguez’s interim administration
He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade.
Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of Trump

articles.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
articles.description:
Estonian completed first of two attempts to navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace on Thursday
The lunchtime crowds drifted slowly back to their offices along central Seoul’s main boulevard, heads up and phones raised to the sky.
High above, a narrow ribbon ran between the Koreana hotel and the Dong-A Media Center, a few hundred metres from the capital’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace and Gwanghwamun square.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Daredevil Jaan Roose completes slackline walk high above central Seoul

articles.author: Lorenzo Tondo and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem; graphics by Ana Lucía González Paz
articles.description:
Some on streets of Jerusalem pledge their support to prime minister while others hope for change
On the streets of Jerusalem, crowded with secular and ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious nationalists, settlers, Palestinians, and soldiers returning from deployments, uncertainty hangs over an election less than a month away that could mark a turning point for a country profoundly changed after the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 and nearly three years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The political battle remains on a knife-edge.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israelis divided as vote that could oust Netanyahu only weeks away

articles.author: Jason Burke and Eithne Staunton
articles.description:
Satellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefire 
An update to Google Maps has revealed the extent of devastation during the three-year Gaza war and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants.
The images were taken in June this year and show further destruction of homes, businesses, places of worship and infrastructure since a fragile ceasefire came into effect almost 12 months ago.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza

articles.author: Andrew Roth and Joseph Gedeon in Washington
articles.description:
Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.
On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi
articles.description:
Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago
The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women
South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.
Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings

articles.author: Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent
articles.description:
Institutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mounting

MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research

The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival.
The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities

articles.author: Vikram Dodd, Sally Weale, Simon Goodley and Richard Adams
articles.description:
Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence

MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities

MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.
Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT).
Additional reporting by Helena Horton
 Continue reading...
articles.title: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy
Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.
However, Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US

articles.author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
articles.description:
Kenjiro Tsuda wins case against TikTok account in landmark Japanese verdict to protect publicity rights
A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos.
Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rules

articles.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
articles.description:
Blast during search operation near border fuels political tensions amid attempts to revive diplomatic channels
South Korea has demanded an apology from North Korea over a landmine blast that injured three soldiers, saying they were hurt by North Korean mines on the southern side of the border.
Kang Hyun-woo, the director of operations at South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff, demanded an apology and “responsible measures” from Pyongyang over the blast, which occurred on 21 September during a search operation south of the border.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South Korea calls for apology from North Korea after mine injures three soldiers

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
As outrage grows over cases​ of sexual violence, activists are demanding a shift from controlling women to confronting men’s behaviour. Plus, Tony Klor’s ‘hella dope’ city vlogs
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
As an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.
Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamui went viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedly gang-raped in a park by men posing as police. After, women in Bihar told Outlook how the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on women

articles.author: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies
articles.description:
Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says

A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.
Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New York
Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king of the world”, has died aged 91.
Francisco, who got his breakthrough in calypso music with his 1956 hit song Jean and Dinah, died peacefully surrounded by his family in New York on Sunday, his family said in a statement.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Hurricane Nolo is moving away from Hawaiian islands but threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists
Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted in areas of the island chain still recovering from previous storms.
Nolo was about 365 miles (585km) south-south-west of Honolulu and moving away from the Big Island at about 12mph (19km/h). But the Hawaii county civil defense agency said a high wind warning, wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening as Nolo’s maximum sustained winds rose to 115mph.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico’s Baja braces for Hurricane Polo

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies
articles.description:
Seventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue near Cape Town
Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, as the country grapples with one of the world’s highest murder rates amid investigations into corruption and criminality within the police.
The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say

articles.author: Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
Loved ones describe Jordan Yap, 30, as an experienced hiker who set out for a 10-day solo trek Peru before falling silent

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Loved ones of a missing Australian trekker who was last seen nearly two weeks ago on a remote South American hiking trail are urging local authorities to help with the search.
A wide-scale sweep by a private rescue crew has so far failed to find any trace of 30-year-old Jordan Yap, who last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Melbourne man’s mysterious disappearance on popular Peru hiking trail prompts widespread search

articles.author: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad and Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Tens of thousands of police deployed and roads barricaded as PTI party demands release of jailed former PM
Leaders from Imran Khan’s party have vowed to go ahead with a nationwide demonstration in Pakistan to demand the former prime minister’s release, even as the government deployed tens of thousands of police to Islamabad, barricaded highways and issued arrest warrants to try to stop the march.
The state has taken extreme measures to prevent Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party from proceeding with the march. It was announced after mounting concerns of the treatment of Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pakistan locks down Islamabad as Imran Khan’s party vows to march on capital

articles.author: Rachel Hall and Patrick Greenfield
articles.description:
Role for Anant Ambani, son of India’s richest person, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo, met with incredulity
Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Backlash as Indian oil heir made professor of sustainability by Newcastle University

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Democratic-led coalition says gutting key protections will set US back decades and worsen climate crisis
States and cities sued the Trump administration on Thursday for repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas.
Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule. The Democratic-led coalition also includes Pennsylvania’s governor, the District of Columbia, New York City, Chicago and the city and county of Denver. They argue that “gutting one of the country’s most significant climate protections” will set the nation back decades and worsen the climate crisis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US states and cities sue over Trump EPA’s repeal of emissions rules

articles.author: Adam Morton, Graham Readfearn and Penry Buckley
articles.description:
Exclusive: Climate Change Authority chair says planning commission did not account for climate-related economic damage in NSW

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

A senior Albanese government climate adviser has challenged the state approval of the largest coalmining development in New South Wales’s history, arguing “climate change isn’t someone else’s problem”.
Matt Kean, the chair of the Climate Change Authority and a former NSW treasurer and energy minister, questioned why the state Independent Planning Commission had not weighed the economic cost of climate change caused by burning the coal from the Hunter Valley Operations mine before giving it the green light to run until 2045.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Matt Kean warns climate crisis ‘isn’t someone else’s problem’ as largest coal project in NSW history greenlit

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description:
As the midterms approach, Americans’ digestive health has become a bizarre talking point
Donald Trump seems to spend an unusual amount of time thinking about toilets.
Back in 2019, he bizarrely claimed: “People are flushing toilets 10 times, 15 times as opposed to once.” He repeated this claim at a Michigan rally the following year. “Ten times, right, 10 times,” Trump complained. “Not me, of course not me, but you,” he added while pointing at an unfortunate audience member.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is Trump to blame for Americans getting explosive diarrhea? | Arwa Mahdawi

articles.author: Evan Simon of Floodlight
articles.description:
Records show Vineland facility in New Jersey emitted health-harming pollution before regulators stepped in
DataOne, the Microsoft-linked New Jersey datacenter recently hit with a $1m fine for running unpermitted generators, emitted large amounts of health-harming air pollution for nearly a year before state regulators stepped in, according to public records obtained by Floodlight.
The Vineland facility’s 62 gas-fired generators became public in August after a Floodlight/Guardian visual investigation found them operating without permits. The New Jersey department of environmental protection last week fined the company over the fleet but did not disclose how long the generators had been operating nor how much air pollution they had released into the surrounding community over the past year.
This story is from Floodlight, a non-profit newsroom that investigates the powers stalling climate action. Sign up for Floodlight’s newsletter here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US datacenter discharged large amounts of pollution for almost a year with no permits

articles.author: Oliver Milman
articles.description:
Gavin Newsom says Trump is a ‘gift’ to the climate cause for dispelling notions of fossil fuel energy security

Send us your questions about how the Iran war will affect US voters in the midterms

Of all the epithets hurled at Donald Trump since he became US president, perhaps the most unusual was delivered last week – that he is, in fact, some sort of environmentalist.
Trump is the “greatest gift” to the environmental movement, argued Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, due to the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump the environmentalist? How his Iran war exposed the fragility of dirty energy

articles.author: Guardian community team
articles.description:
Our wildlife series Young Country Diary is looking for articles written by children, about their autumn encounters with nature 
Once again, the Young Country Diary series is open for submissions! Every three months we ask you to send us an article written by a child aged 8-14.
The article needs to be about a recent encounter they’ve had with nature – whether it’s a hedge full of berries, a beetle on the move, or a nervous deer.

articles.title: Nature boys and girls – here’s your chance to get published in the Guardian

articles.author: Kate Ravilious
articles.description:
Some rivers are receiving more rain than before but have lower water flow, according to a study
More rain and snow equals more water in rivers, right? Not necessarily. A new study shows that, despite receiving more rainfall than they used to, river water levels are falling because of changes in climate.
Global heating is intensifying the hydrological cycle, making wet regions wetter and dry regions drier, but how is this affecting river flow? Researchers from the Pennsylvania State University, in the US, have analysed precipitation and river flow records in more than 10,000 rivers between 1951 and 2020. In nearly one-third of rivers, they found that flow trends did not match with the changes observed in rainfall and snow.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Think more rain means more river water? Not necessarily

articles.author: Ajit Niranjan
articles.description:
Alpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution
Switzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years, research has found, in a dramatic reshaping of the Alpine country whose big white glaciers have been reduced to moonlike rock deserts, scientists say.
Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and brings the total loss of glacier ice since 2021 to 19.4%.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years

articles.author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
articles.description:
The global climate phenomenon has triggered devastating infernos in the ape’s Indonesian heartlands, with long-term effects on the animals still unknown
The mother’s hands were peeling from walking on the torched ground. Her eight-month-old baby, which clung to her side, was dehydrated and thin. The pair, named Mama Abu and Abu (“ash” in Indonesian), were found in an oil palm subsidiary estate, rescuers say.
The orangutan pair were saved last month from wildfires that are devouring Indonesia’s forests and peatland, unleashing thick smog, and destroying the habitat of some of the planet’s most vulnerable species.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘The toll is huge’: El Niño-driven wildfires overwhelm Indonesia’s orangutan population

articles.author: Georgina Woods
articles.description:
There is no greater treachery than this failure to face up to the climate crisis. How can we now fend off despair?
The Independent Planning Commission’s published reasons for approving the largest coalmine in New South Wales history in the context of mounting death, disaster and despair brought on by global heating reads like a hostage statement.
In its decision, the commission accepts that the extension of the Hunter Valley Operations’ mine for a further 19 years – resulting 809m tonnes of greenhouse gas pollution – will materially worsen global warming. The panel members cite CSIRO’s finding that climate change is having a growing effect on the lives and livelihoods of all Australians and that the severity of that impact “will depend on the speed at which global greenhouse gas emissions can be reduced”. They reject the idea that keeping HVO’s coal in the ground would make no difference to global warming.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The green light for the largest coalmine in NSW history is shocking proof that our governance systems are betraying Australians | Georgina Woods

articles.author: Editorial
articles.description:
Sunday’s general election is too close to call, with the incumbent president facing the son of the man who attempted a coup against him
Sunday’s election in Brazil could hardly be a clearer-cut choice – nor a closer call. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, is neck and neck in the polls with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son and champion of the jailed far-right former president Jair. Mr Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to “annihilate” democracy after losing the last election.
Brazil is Latin America’s largest democracy, but military dictatorship is in its recent past. Mr Bolsonaro wants to free his father and those who rioted in his support in 2023. The senator has campaigned as a less crass and temperamental version of his father, but he is no less extreme. For many on both sides, this is a vote against a man they detest more than an endorsement of their own candidate. Most voters disapprove of both men.
Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.

articles.title: The Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us all | Editorial

articles.author: Gabrielle Canon in San Francisco
articles.description:
Wave nearing southern California expected to reach San Francisco Bay Area by October as it crawls toward Alaska
Communities across California are rushing to prepare for the imminent arrival of the so-called “Kelvin wave”, a massive underwater band of warm water threatening to inundate swaths of the vast North American shoreline.
The wave is nearing southern California and expected to reach the San Francisco Bay Area by early October, as it crawls toward Alaska. Waters could rise by a foot along the California coast, according to scientists, who have warned that this could dramatically double the 8-12in rise in sea levels already caused by climate change over the last century.

articles.title: California rushes to prepare for massive ‘Kelvin’ wave and predicted sea level rise

articles.description:
Insects provide protection, sanitation and even shelter to vertebrates, making them a priority for conservation efforts
For many vertebrates, insects are more than a food source. As “little things that run the world”, insects provide critical functions such as protection, sanitation and shelter across ecosystems, according to a new study.
The study, published in Nature Reviews Biodiversity on Wednesday, sheds light on the various ways insects support vertebrates, ranging from birds and bats to reptiles, amphibians and mammals.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Insects play critical role in ecosystems beyond just providing food, new research shows

articles.author: Karen McVeigh
articles.description:
Fish and shellfish populations were falling rapidly as scallop dredgers devastated the seabed, but local activists and small-scale fishers battled hard to protect their coastline
Inside a bothy overlooking the Summer Isles, in the north-west of Scotland, the lilting tones of a traditional Gaelic duo fill a room full of musicians, storytellers, artists, local people and revellers, hung with fish-shaped lanterns and “Happy Birthday” signs.
It’s no ordinary birthday. The people in the small cabin have come together, on a windy night in Achiltibuie, a string of coastal hamlets and villages north of Ullapool, to celebrate an important milestone in the community’s history: a hard-won battle to protect their waters from the ravages of scallop dredging.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Beyond priceless’: how a halt to dredging saved the seas of Scotland’s Summer Isles

articles.author: Michael Sainato
articles.description:
Federal workers’ union alleges EPA illegally terminated agreement with the goal of repressing political dissent
The union representing more than 8,000 workers at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) filed a lawsuit against the agency and administrator Lee Zeldin on Tuesday alleging the agency illegally terminated the union’s collective bargaining agreement.
The lawsuit, filed by two local unions of the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), claims the agency failed to justify the contract’s termination and was motivated by a desire to repress political dissent, a violation of the employees’ first amendment rights.

articles.title: EPA union sues Trump administration to restore collective bargaining contract

articles.author: Matthew Pearce
articles.description:
Indigenous communities play crucial role, as ‘genetic bank’ area of wetland offers hope for critically endangered reptile
In the 1990s, conservationists in Cambodia feared the Siamese crocodile had disappeared for good. Fishing and hunting had devastated the species throughout the 20th century, leaving populations across its native south-east Asia on the brink of extinction.
But in villages dotted among the wetlands of the remote Cardamom mountains, Indigenous Chorng communities still reported seeing them. Passing this knowledge to researchers surveying the area in 2000 led to an official recording of the species – and bolstered the mission to revive the population.

articles.title: Saving the Siamese crocodile: Cambodia moves to protect one of the world’s last wild populations

articles.author: Gloria Dickie
articles.description:
Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer
Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.
Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

Authorities declared a flood disaster across Bangkok after almost two days of heavy rain left homes, shops and roads waterlogged and residents wading through waist-deep water.
The Thai capital recorded 300mm of rainfall over 48 hours through ⁠Saturday in some areas, flooding roads and ​leaving ​some cars ​submerged. The rain swelled the city’s network of canals, sending murky water into surrounding homes, restaurants and shops

articles.author: Editorial
articles.description:
Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice
Some warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions of a super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niño already heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high.
The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger. Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause the deaths of 450,000 people by February, from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination | Editorial

articles.author: Nick Dall
articles.description:
Known as the ‘energy bars of the sea’ the fish are a key food source for many species, but closing fisheries to allow numbers to recover would cost millions 
It began on 28 July, when fishers near Saldanha Bay on the west coast of South Africa reported seeing dead sardines (also known as pilchards) floating at sea. Then, in early August, more dead sardines began washing up on beaches near Cape Town.
In the weeks that followed, similar reports came in from places across a vast area spanning 2,600km (1,600 miles) of coastline, such as Henties Bay in Namibia and Mbotyi in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa.

articles.description:
Biggest study of its kind provides insights into bats’ evolution – a potential gamechanger for research into treating viruses and cancer in humans

In the northern forests of the Congo-Brazzaville, as the sun slips away, a distinctive honking fills the dusky sky. Every evening, thousands of hammer-headed fruit bats depart their daytime roosts in search of mates, calling out through large, box-shaped snouts that give the flying mammals the appearance of a winged moose. Here, along the Congo River, scientists have been collecting DNA swabs and tissue samples from the bats for years, working deep into the night in spacesuit-like protective gear.
Those hard-won samples are now among the thousands of specimens gathered from bats across the world that have helped to reshape what we know about the bat family tree.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bats originated in Europe, rewriting mammals’ family tree, study reveals

articles.author: Bill McKibben
articles.description:
There is hope in solar power. As the UN meets, we are urging leaders to pursue a clear goal: clean energy for all by 2030

Our message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s end

As climate experts from around the world gather in New York for their annual week of talking through the world’s deepest dilemma, the vibes are mostly bad.
Though 2026 seems likely to set a new global temperature record (and 2027, as El Niño gathers steam, is almost certain to break it), and though the planet has careened from one climate disaster to another (European heatwaves that killed tens of thousands, a Nepali flood that wiped out entire communities), and though scientists warn that we’re reaching precisely the global tipping points they’ve long feared (the new research on the faltering great currents of the Atlantic should send a literal chill up your spine), there’s a distinct lack of political momentum.
The path forward is difficult, but the way is clear. We want solar for everyone, everywhere, before the decade is out.
We know that standing up to the powerful can be scary. But if there is one thing that unites us, it is that we live beneath the same sun. That unity is our strength, and we must use it to act now.
Bill McKibben is the Schumann distinguished scholar at Middlebury College. He is the founder of Third Act, organizing people over 60 for progressive change
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The climate fight has one great ally. You just can’t look at it directly | Bill McKibben

articles.author: Karen McVeigh
articles.description:
A magical new film captures the secret life of the deep sea in a stretch of the ocean at risk from industrial mining
A magical film that explores the wonders of the deep sea through the eyes of a team of scientists and an underwater robot called Isis will be shown in selected cinemas across the UK next month.
The documentary, How Deep Is Your Love, offers a playful, irreverent and bittersweet look at our anthropocentric view of Earth, as it switches perspective from humans to deep sea animals and back again.
